confirmed.statement: The document says assignment was random in one place: 'Each student solved one problem only and was randomly assigned the method to use, either TRIZ-C+LLM or TRIZ-C.' A full-text search finds no other use of 'random', and the paper describes no procedure, balance check, or preregistration. The form records the missing procedure, and randomized = yes stands.
confirmed.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Section 3.2.1; full text, pp. 507-516

confirmed.statement: The form's assignment quote is verbatim, and its locator (p. 510, Section 3.2.1, with groups and locations in Figure 2) is right. No preregistration is mentioned, so preregistered = not_stated is right.

Each student used one method on one problem and worked alone ('conducted with individual students rather than teams'). So unit = individual and structure = between are right, and no within-person order needs checking.
confirmed.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Section 3.2.1; p. 514 (PDF p. 8), Section 5.1

confirmed.statement: Only the method was randomized. The problem followed the group: 'Group 2 corresponds to the students solving the GT problem, Group 3 to the students solving the MB problems, Group 4 to the students solving the WT problem.' Figure 2 puts Groups 2 and 3 at Location 2 and Group 4 at Location 3, and splits each group into both arms. GT and MB 'were part of a course'. This matches what_was_assigned.
confirmed.locator: p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Section 3.2.1, Table 1, and Figure 2

confirmed.statement: What was assigned is AI help on the student's own work, not a change in whose output is rated. TRIZ-C+LLM students used the LLM to search for contradictions and for specific solutions, then developed their most promising solution. TRIZ-C students did each step manually. Experts then rated the students' solutions.

confirmed.statement: The tool is generative AI. The method is 'the TRIZ contradiction matrix with the support of LLM-based artificial intelligence (AI) assistants, also called chatbots'. Students were recommended 'Microsoft Copilot with the LLM option Smart GPT-5' and were free to choose other LLM-based assistants if they reported which one. The paper never names the assistants used (Section 5.1 mentions only 'various LLM-based AI assistants'). This matches ai_tool.name_model.
confirmed.locator: p. 508 (PDF p. 2), Section 1; p. 511 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.3; p. 514 (PDF p. 8), Section 5.1

confirmed.statement: The prompt pack in arms[TRIZ-C+LLM] and ai_tool.how_used matches the paper: instructions and examples for problem framing, contradiction parameters, inventive principles, solution generation, and a diversity check. ai_tool.role = open_chat fits, because students used a general chatbot of their choice with suggested prompts.

Comparison arm: TRIZ-C students 'were given access to the https://www.triz40.com/ site and were asked to not use any LLM-based AI assistants', and RQ1 calls this arm 'TRIZ contradictions alone'. So arms[TRIZ-C].ai = none fits. The paper does not say what the site holds or whether the LLM arm also had it. Both methods are defined as uses of the TRIZ contradiction matrix, so the site reads as the control arm's copy of the shared method, not an extra aid, and ai_vs_bau stands.
confirmed.locator: p. 511 (PDF p. 5), Section 3.3; p. 508 (PDF p. 2), Section 1 and RQ1

confirmed.statement: The paper reports no compliance check. TRIZ-C students were only 'asked' not to use LLMs, and LLM-arm students 'could' leave their prompts. Before the test, all participants had the same TRIZ and prompt-engineering introductions and a practice problem on 'TRIZ steps, and LLM use'. The control arm may have tried an LLM in practice, but its scored task was done without one. This does not change the coding.
confirmed.locator: p. 511 (PDF p. 5), Sections 3.2.3 and 3.3, and Figure 3

confirmed.statement: Analyzed counts match arms[].n_analyzed: TRIZ-C 51 (GT 11, MB 10, WT 30) and TRIZ-C+LLM 63 (GT 10, MB 10, WT 43), total 114. The paper prints no count at assignment and does not give the excluded GT student's arm, so n_randomized = null is right.
confirmed.locator: p. 512 (PDF p. 6), Table 2; p. 510 (PDF p. 4), Table 1 note

confirmed.statement: GT (11 vs 10) and MB (10 vs 10) are near-even. The WT split (43 vs 30) is uneven, but under simple 1:1 assignment a split at least this uneven has an exact two-sided binomial probability of 0.16 (this check's computation, not the paper's). So the split does not undercut the claim of random assignment.

summary: The PDF supports every part of the assignment, arms, and ai_tool coding: each student 'was randomly assigned the method to use, either TRIZ-C+LLM or TRIZ-C' (p. 510, Section 3.2.1), the LLM arm used a chatbot (Microsoft Copilot with Smart GPT-5 recommended) on the student's own solution, the TRIZ-C arm was asked not to use any LLM (p. 511, Section 3.3), and 63 and 51 students were analyzed (p. 512, Table 2). The weaknesses leave criterion 1 intact: the paper gives no randomization procedure or count at assignment and ties each problem to one student group, which the form records, and it reports no check that students kept to their assigned method.
